case_studies.title: Optimize the Harness, Not the Model: Fitting a Minimal Agent to a Self-Hostable LLM for Investigative Analysis
case_studies.abstract: Government intelligence teams need LLM agents that can analyze large, messy evidence collections, but security and cost constraints often rule out hosted frontier models and broad, hard-to-audit tool surfaces. We report CLEO: Constrained Loop for Environment Optimization, a method for fitting a minimal agent harness to a fixed, self-hostable LLM. Given an expert-validated dataset, CLEO admits only the tools, guardrails, memory policies, and loop components that improve accuracy while remaining general and auditable. On our held-out dataset, the CLEO harness reaches an 83.8% pass rate, within 1.2 points of the strongest out-of-the-box Claude Code SDK baseline, while being two orders of magnitude smaller.
case_studies.summary: CLEO builds a tiny, self‑hosted AI harness that keeps only the tools and rules that actually improve accuracy, achieving an 83.8% pass rate—just 1.2 points shy of a top commercial model—while being 100× smaller.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infra and run in‑house LLMs, check if your current tool stack can be trimmed to the minimal set that CLEO recommends: step 1, audit the tools your LLM uses; step 2, replace or remove any that do not directly contribute to accuracy; step 3, test the trimmed harness on a validation set to confirm performance is retained.
case_studies.relevance_tag: cloud, on-prem, LLM deployment, security, devops
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a practical method (CLEO) for fitting minimal, self-hostable LLM agents suitable for secure, cost‑constrained environments, directly relevant to IT engineers managing on‑prem or hybrid deployments. The approach is reported as deployed and evaluated, indicating high maturity. The harness can be adopted or offered as a service within 90 days, providing clear monetisation potential.

case_studies.title: IAMRAGBENCH: Benchmarking Authorization Expansions in LLM-Generated AWS IAM Policies under RAG Poisoning
case_studies.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can synthesize Amazon Web Services (AWS) Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies from tasks and operational documents. Attacker-controlled context may induce provider-valid policies that exceed trusted authorization requirements. We present IAMRAGBENCH, a 60-case benchmark spanning scope, conditions, explicit denies, trust, permissions boundaries, and role delegation. It combines deterministic authorization-envelope scoring with case-specific validation, including request-level checks where supported. An attack requires a provider-valid clean policy that satisfies the task and a provider-valid treatment policy that violates the envelope, matches a predeclared goal, preserves an intended request, and newly authorizes a forbidden request. Across five endpoints, included-context exposure produces 49 exact authorization deltas, including 46 goal-matched attacks (46/292; 15.75\%). End-to-end BM25 over 720 documents retrieves the designated poison for all 60 tasks at \(k=5\) but produces 7/294 goal-matched attacks (2.38\%). Presenting the same weakening as a final security architecture exception produces 74/116 attacks in a frozen two-endpoint stress test (63.79\%) and 115/294 in a post hoc all-five extension using the same frozen prompts (39.12\%). In a replay of 194 provider-valid treatment policies that violate task requirements, AWS \texttt{CheckNoNewAccess} reports no new access for four of 168 goal-matched exact attacks. The full pre-deployment rule rejects all 171 exact deltas and routes five unresolved cases to review. These findings support treating IAM copilots as untrusted proposal generators whose outputs require independent authorization checks before deployment.
case_studies.summary: This research shows that LLMs using RAG can generate valid AWS IAM policies that unintentionally grant extra permissions. The authors built IAMRAGBENCH, a benchmark of 60 policy cases, and found that up to 15.8% of attacks succeed when attackers poison the context. The study highlights the risk of trusting LLM-generated IAM policies without verification.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AWS IAM, immediately enforce independent policy review: 1) run any LLM‑generated policy through AWS CheckNoNewAccess; 2) compare the policy against an authorization envelope; 3) block deployment if any new permissions are detected.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The benchmark directly impacts AWS IAM policy management for IT engineers, providing a practical tool to detect mis‑generated policies. It is a published dataset with code and evaluation scripts, making it usable now, though not a full product. The findings can be turned into a quick‑start testing service or an audit plugin that IT teams can deploy within weeks, giving clear commercial value.

case_studies.title: VeriHarm-Bench: Measuring Harmful Success in LLM Coding Agents Verifiably
case_studies.abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents increasingly operate with shell access, allowing them to write scripts, move files, alter permissions, and modify system configurations. However, an agent may achieve a user's goal while causing unintended harm, such as deleting unrelated files, weakening access controls, or corrupting data, in response to benign inputs without explicit jailbreaking. This failure mode is particularly important because apparent task success may reassure users that an agent behaved correctly, causing harmful side effects to go unnoticed. We call this harmful success: the agent successfully completes the intended benign task while simultaneously causing unintended harm. Despite its importance, harmful success is difficult to measure because conventional task-success metrics overlook harmful behaviors, while existing safety evaluations are often designed solely to assess harmful outcomes. We introduce VeriHarm, an automatic framework for constructing programmatically verifiable benchmarks that directly measure harmful success. VeriHarm minimally perturbs coding tasks to elicit unintended harmful behavior while maintaining the benignity of the task and preserving the original task objective. It then synthesizes executable harm tests that, together with the original task-correctness tests, evaluate both task accuracy and harmful outcomes. Frontier agents, including GPT-5.6-Sol and Claude-Opus-5, achieve an average task accuracy of 95% on our curated VeriHarm-Bench, yet still struggle to complete tasks safely: their safe success rate, the fraction of tasks completed successfully without triggering the designated harm, averages only 37%. These results suggest that successful task completion can frequently coexist with unintended harm, and that task-success metrics alone may substantially understate the potential safety risks of coding agents.
case_studies.summary: VeriHarm-Bench shows that LLM coding agents can finish tasks but still delete files, weaken permissions, or corrupt data. The researchers built an automated test framework that adds hidden harm tests to regular coding tasks, revealing that top agents only avoid harm 37% of the time. This matters for cloud managers because unseen damage can slip through during automation.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, check if your automated code agents run with shell access – add VeriHarm-style hidden harm tests to your CI pipeline to catch unintended file deletions or permission changes. If your org uses LLM agents for script generation, audit their outputs for side‑effects before deployment. If you don’t run such agents, no immediate action is needed.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces VeriHarm, a framework to measure harmful success in LLM coding agents. This is directly relevant to IT engineers who deploy such agents for automation, scripting, and system configuration, providing a new metric that can flag unintended side effects. The framework appears to be a working prototype with released code, making it mature enough for real-world testing. It offers clear, actionable tests that can be integrated into existing security or DevOps pipelines, enabling engineers to assess and mitigate risks quickly, and could be packaged as a SaaS testing service. The total score is 45, well above the threshold for low signal.

case_studies.title: Can LLM Agents Be Forward-Deployed Engineers? Requirement Discovery and Delivery for Enterprise Text-to-SQL
case_studies.abstract: LLM coding agents can increasingly automate model post-training, but whether they can act as forward-deployed engineer (FDE) agents, discovering customer requirements and turning them into deployment decisions, remains unclear. We study this on a real enterprise text-to-SQL engagement: a simulated customer, grounded in the real use case's requirements, starts with an ambiguous request. An agent must discover acceptance criteria, data permissions, and hardware constraints in the discovery phase, then plan and execute a post-training recipe in the delivery phase. Across 15 models, the strongest discover over 80% of withheld requirements and open-weight models discover 40-50%; in the delivery phase, only 25% of runs across eight coding-agent configurations pass all acceptance criteria. We identify four bottlenecks in this engagement: (1) incomplete discovery, with 40% of withheld requirements missing or misrepresented; (2) unreliable execution; (3) underused compute budgets and a lack of systematic comparisons across base models and post-training methods; and (4) benchmark accuracy does not guarantee production readiness. We suggest human review of discovered requirements, monitoring of the agent's plan during execution, and an explicit experiment-environment specification covering hardware, budget scope, and production checks.
case_studies.summary: The study shows LLM agents can help discover and deliver SQL queries for business data, but they struggle with incomplete requirement discovery, unreliable execution, and unclear hardware constraints. They built a simulation of an enterprise text‑to‑SQL engagement and found that only about a quarter of runs met all acceptance criteria, highlighting gaps that limit production use. This research points to a risk for cloud infrastructure managers who rely on automated code generation.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure for data services, check whether your deployment pipelines include manual review steps for requirement discovery, monitor execution logs for reliability, and set explicit compute‑budget and production‑readiness tests before trusting an LLM to automate SQL generation.
case_studies.relevance_tag: LLM-based automation for enterprise data engineering
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses LLM agents for requirement discovery and deployment in enterprise SQL contexts, relevant to IT engineers. However it is an experimental study with limited practical deployment evidence, and monetisation is unclear. Overall moderate impact, low maturity, and low immediate commercial value.
